'''Roger N. Beachy''' is an American [[biologist]] and member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] who studies plant virology. He was the founding president of the [[Donald Danforth Plant Science Center]] in St. Louis, Missouri, and the first director of the [[National Institute of Food and Agriculture]].

== Birth, family and education ==
Roger N. Beachy was born in 1944 in [[Plain City, Ohio]]. His father was a mennonite minister who left school in the 8th grade.<ref name="PNASPodcast">{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/podcasts/interviews/roger-beachy.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905205718/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/podcasts/interviews/roger-beachy.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 5, 2015|title = Roger Beachy}}</ref><ref name="STLInterview">{{Cite web|url=https://www.stlmag.com/A-Conversation-With-Roger-Beachy-President-of-the-Donald-Danforth-Plant-Science-Center/|title = A Conversation with Roger Beachy, President Emeritus of the Donald Danforth Plant Science Center|date = 17 February 2012}}</ref> He became interested in plant biology as a high school student at [[Bethany Christian Schools]] in [[Goshen, Indiana]]. In 1966, he completed his BA at [[Goshen College]] in Goshen, Indiana.<ref name="PNASPodcast" /> He then would complete a Ph.D. in plant pathology at [[Michigan State University]] in 1973. Beachy began a postdoc in the lab of [[Milton Zaitlin]] at the [[University of Arizona]] for nine months when Prof. Zaitlin moved the entire research group to [[Cornell University]], where Beachy remained for another four years.<ref name="PNASPodcast" />

== Academic career ==

In 1978, Beachy was hired as an assistant professor in the Biology Department of [[Washington University in St. Louis]]. He remained at Washington University, being promoted to associate and then full professor and becoming the head of the Center for Plant Science and Biotechnology, until 1991.<ref name="USDALecture">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ars.usda.gov/northeast-area/docs/distinguished-lecture/roger-beachy/|title = Roger Beachy : USDA ARS}}</ref> From 1991 to 1998, he was the head of the Plant Biology division of [[Scripps Research|Scripps Research Institute]]. In 1999, he was recruited to be the inaugural president of the [[Donald Danforth Plant Science Center]] in [[St. Louis, MO]] as well as resuming his appointment with Washington University. He left the Danforth Center in 2009 when he was appointed as the director of the [[National Institute of Food and Agriculture]] by [[President Obama]], a role he served in until 2011.<ref name="NSFBio"/> He also served on the Life Sciences jury for the [[Infosys Prize]] in 2009. From 2014-2020, he was a member of the [[National Science Board]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/staff/staff_list.jsp?orgId=496&subDiv=y&org=NSB&from_org=NSF|title = Terms expire May 10, 2026 () Staff &#124; NSF - National Science Foundation}}</ref>

== Research ==
Beachy is a plant virologist whose research focused on molecular mechanisms of plant–virus interactions and the development of virus-resistant crops through genetic engineering.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|title=Delay of Disease Development in Transgenic Plants That Express the Tobacco Mosaic Virus Coat Protein Gene|last=Abel|first=P|date=1986-05-09|journal=Science|issue=4751|volume=232|pages=738-743|doi=10.1126/science.3457472}}</ref> His work helped establish pathogen-derived resistance as a general strategy for protecting plants from viral disease.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Pathogen-Derived Resistance to Plant Viruses|last=Lomonossoff|first=GP|date=1995-09-01|journal=Annual Review of Phytopathology|volume=33|pages=323-343|doi=10.1146/annurev.py.33.090195.001543}}</ref>

His research at [[Washington University in St. Louis]], in collaboration with Monsanto Company, led to the development of the world’s first [[Genetically modified food|genetically modified food crop]], a variety of tomato that was modified for resistance to virus disease.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.stlmag.com/A-Conversation-With-Roger-Beachy-President-of-the-Donald-Danforth-Plant-Science-Center/|title=A Conversation With Roger Beachy, President Emeritus of the Donald Danforth Plant Science Center|date=2012-02-17|access-date=2026-01-29|website=St Louis Magazine|last=Cooperman|first=Jeannette}}</ref> His research demonstrated resistance to viral infection could be achieved by expressing viral coat protein genes in transgenic plants, a phenomenon later termed coat protein–mediated resistance.<ref name=":0" /> This approach provided a molecular basis for engineering virus resistance and was subsequently applied to multiple crop species, including tomato, potato, pepper, papaya, and squash, contributing to the broader adoption of virus-resistant transgenic plants.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=The Impact of “Coat Protein-Mediated Virus Resistance” in Applied Plant Pathology and Basic Research|last=Linbo|first=JA|date=2017-06-01|journal=Phytopathology|issue=6|volume=107|pages=624-634|last2=Falk|first2=BW|doi=10.1094/PHYTO-12-16-0442-RVW}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==

* Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (1987)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/listing|title=Elected Fellows &#124; American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS)|website=www.aaas.org|accessdate=1 June 2023}}</ref>
* Elected a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1997.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/roger-n-beachy-zwttc7/|title = Roger N. Beachy}}</ref>
* Recipient of the 2001 [[Wolf Prize in Agriculture]] with [[James E. Womack]] "for the use of recombinant DNA technology, to revolutionize plant and animal sciences, paving the way for applications to neighboring fields".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wolffund.org.il/2018/12/10/roger-n-beachy/|title = Roger N. Beachy| work=Wolf Foundation |date = 10 December 2018}}</ref>
